newsitem.title: CHINA: China bans Chinese from buying new B shares.
newsitem.headline: China bans Chinese from buying new B shares.

text.p: China's Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges have banned domestic investors from buying new foreign currency B shares, the China Securities newspaper said on Saturday.
Analysts said the order would deal a heavy blow to both B share markets, where local Chinese accounts for about half of the trading, and would drive the Shanghai index to record lows.

"The ban is a new blow to the B share markets, already in depression for two years," said one stock analyst. "Shanghai's B share index, lingering around historical lows, is likely to hit record lows in the next few days because of the ban."
The newspaper said the two exchanges took the step after the China Securities Regulatory Commisssion (CSRC) reaffirmed an existing ban in June on mainland Chinese trading B shares.
The newspaper said the two exchanges in separate notices issued on Friday said that existing domestic investors must not buy any new B shares with immediate effect.
They can still sell B shares they hold and enjoy the rights of B share investors before all their shares are sold, it said. The exchanges did not set a deadline.
"The exchange will take appropriate technical measures to enforce the ban," the notice by the Shanghai exchange published in the Shanghai Securities News said.

China's securities rules on B share trading which came into effect early this year defined those allowed to hold B shares -- citizens and institutions of foreign countries, of Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan and Chinese living permanently abroad.
But, in practice, about 50 percent of the B share trading in the two bourses has been done by domestic investors.

China established the B share markets in 1992 and, in the first two years, the B shares were solely in the hands of foreign investors. But a market slump in mid-1994 made the two exchanges relax controls in order to stimulate trading.
Many domestic investors took advantage of this to enter the B share market where share prices are at a huge discount against their domestic equivalent.

Analysts believe the securities authorities chose this moment to implement the ban because China's economy is improving with a gradual relaxation in a three-year austerity programme, which is likely to improve the performance of listed companies.
Poor company results have been the most important reason for the B share market slump in the past two years.

"The timing was carefully chosen," said a second analyst. "With company performance likely to get better along with the improvement of the national economy, the authorities believe there will be less negative impact."

Another reason for announcing the ban at this moment is that, during a rebound in the Shanghai and Shenzhen B market in June, some foreigners took the opportunity to sell to domestic investors B shares whose prices have since fallen.
"Beijing saw this as a loss of foreign exchange, with the foreigners selling at a high level and the Chinese investor being left with the cheaper share," the second analyst said.
Shanghai's B share index closed at 49.346 points on Friday against a 1996 high of 54.466 points in mid-June.
In Shenzhen, the B index has fell to 87.36 points on Friday from a 1996 high of 116.55 points in mid-June.
